problem: Monolithic whole-body policies for legged loco-manipulation must fuse heterogeneous locomotion and manipulation observations and control regimes, which makes them hard to train and brittle out of distribution. Decoupled policies lose coordination between base and arm.
motivation: A legged base under open-loop velocity commands and a short-reach arm are strongly asymmetric, so base errors disproportionately hurt manipulation. The paper decouples the two subsystems and restores coordination through a shared semantic latent from a frozen foundation model instead of an end-to-end VLA.
key_idea: Train separate diffusion policies for the quadruped base and the arm, both conditioned on a shared CLIP-derived latent that includes language-defined phase/progress signals and is shaped by a coordination-aware contrastive loss.
insight: Decoupling is what makes the task solvable with 50 demos: the centralized baselines (CDP, ACT) get 0% or near-0% overall success on Task 1, while the decoupled methods do far better. Removing the phase/progress head drops Task 1 Left/Right pick-and-place from 60%/100% to 0%/20%, so language-defined phase signals act as a strong inductive bias. The contrastive loss helps in-distribution (Task 1) but slightly hurts base navigation OOD in Task 2, because it couples the base to arm-specific cues.
method: Decoupled diffusion policies: a quadruped diffusion policy outputs velocity, body pitch and height commands, executed open-loop through a pre-trained RL low-level controller; an arm diffusion policy outputs end-effector poses executed via IK. Each uses its own observations.

Shared CLIP latent: frozen CLIP encodes multi-view RGB, proprioception (via an MLP) and the task instruction, fused by a shallow Transformer into h_t (512-d). The result is concatenated with each policy's local observation as conditioning.

Language-defined phase/progress head: hand-written 'ongoing' and 'done' prompts per phase (move, align, place, close) are compared with CLIP image features to give phase probabilities ρ_t and a progress scalar p_t. No phase labels are needed. The conditioning vector is z_t=[h_t,ρ_t,p_t].

Coordination-aware contrastive loss: an InfoNCE loss aligns the observation latent with the coordinated joint arm+base action summary. Negatives are mismatched arm/base pairs made by shuffling across the batch. Total loss = L_diff(arm) + L_diff(quad) + δ·L_coord.
RL low-level controller: PPO-trained in simulation to track velocity, body pitch and height commands, with domain randomization and an added orientation reward. It runs at 50 Hz on the Go2.
Tri-camera RGB-only setup: wrist, body (fisheye) and head cameras, with offboard inference at 10 Hz on an RTX 4090.

setting.backbone: Diffusion policies (arm and quadruped) trained from scratch, with frozen CLIP encoders plus trainable projectors, a Transformer fusion module and a PPO low-level controller
setting.training_data: 50 teleoperated real-robot demonstrations per task; the low-level RL controller is trained in simulation
setting.observation: Three RGB cameras (wrist, head, body fisheye), proprioception (end-effector pose, base state), and a language instruction; no depth
setting.action_space: High-level base velocity, body pitch and height commands to an RL low-level joint controller; arm end-effector Cartesian targets via IK
setting.simulator: Real-world only for the high-level policies (the low-level controller is trained in simulation)

numbers_note: Real-robot manipulation tasks with no canonical navigation benchmark. Task success rates appear mostly in a figure and a stage-wise table. Task 1 stage-wise success rates (FALCON, 5 trials per region): Center 100/100/100/100, Left 100/80/60/60, Right 100/100/100/100. Task 2 reaches 100% overall success per the text.
results: On real-robot tasks with 15 trials each, FALCON beats CDP, ACT and LatentToM. It reaches 100% overall on Task 2, and 100% Place Toy in the Center and Right regions of Task 1 versus 40% and 20% for LatentToM. Centralized ACT never completes either task. In human-in-the-loop tests, FALCON keeps 100% success when paired with a teleoperated counterpart in the reported modes.
limitations: Phase prompts are hand-written and depend on CLIP's reliability, so they are sensitive to prompt quality and visual domain shift.
Only two tasks, 15 trials each with 5 per region, so statistical power is low. They are short-horizon, and the phase set is task-specific.
The contrastive loss can hurt base generalization out of distribution, and the base policy is fragile to camera occlusion.
